title: The big pack can cost more
hook: A larger pack looks like a bargain. What happens per kilogram?
question: A costs €3 for 500g. B costs €6 for 900g. Which costs less per kilogram at B=€6?
assumptions: Scaled model; prices fictional; same product.
details: A costs €3 for 500g. B costs €6 for 900g.
principle: Dividing price by kilograms puts both packs on the same denominator. Pack size alone does not determine unit price; the receipt and quantity must travel together.
objective: Normalize different pack masses to cost per kilogram.
misconception: The largest pack always has the lowest unit price.

recall.question: Fictional packs of the same product: 400g for €2, or 1kg for €6. Which costs less per kilogram?
recall.why: €2 ÷ 0.4kg = €5/kg, below €6/kg: divide price by mass, because pack size alone does not set the unit price.

title: Align the shelf-label units
hook: €0.80 per 100g or €7 per kg: which label is lower?
question: A is €0.80 per 100g. B is €7 per kg. Which unit price is lower at B=€7?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional prices; 1kg=1000g.
details: A is €0.80 per 100g. B is €7 per kg.
principle: A kilogram contains ten 100g units. Multiply the 100g price by ten before comparing. A smaller printed price can describe a smaller amount rather than a cheaper product.
objective: Convert prices quoted per 100g and per kilogram to a common unit.
misconception: The smaller number on a price label is always cheaper.

recall.question: Two fictional shelf labels: €0.65 per 100g and €6 per kg. Which is lower per kilogram?
recall.why: A kilogram is ten 100g units, so €0.65 per 100g is €6.50 per kg; the smaller printed number described a smaller amount.

title: Count sheets, not just rolls
hook: Six rolls or four rolls? The count inside each roll changes the arithmetic.
question: A costs €6: six rolls of 120 sheets. B costs €5: four rolls of 240 sheets. Which costs less per sheet at B=240 sheets/roll?
assumptions: Scaled model; identical sheet size; fictional prices.
details: A costs €6: six rolls of 120 sheets. B costs €5: four rolls of 240 sheets.
principle: The denominator is total sheets: rolls multiplied by sheets per roll. Comparing only roll counts hides the usable quantity. This model assumes equal sheet size and quality.
objective: Calculate the usable unit count inside multipacks before comparing prices.
misconception: More rolls necessarily means more usable paper.

recall.question: Fictional packs: eight rolls of 150 sheets for €6, or four rolls of 300 sheets for €5. Which costs less per sheet?
recall.why: Both packs hold 1,200 sheets (rolls × sheets per roll), so the €5 pack costs less per sheet; the roll count hid that.

title: Two-for-one has a boundary
hook: A promotion can change its effective price when you need an odd quantity.
question: Singles cost €3 each. A two-for-one pair costs €4; pairs are indivisible. For three required items, which checkout is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional offer; pair-only purchase.
details: Singles cost €3 each. A two-for-one pair costs €4; pairs are indivisible.
principle: A pair-only offer bills complete pairs. The ceiling rounds an odd requirement up, so the unneeded extra item still appears on the checkout total.
objective: Account for indivisible promotional bundles and odd demand.
misconception: Two-for-one always halves the checkout cost for the exact quantity needed.

recall.question: Singles cost €3 each; a two-for-one pair costs €4 and pairs cannot be split. You need five items. What does the pairs-only checkout cost?
recall.why: Five items need three whole pairs (rounded up), so you pay €12 including one item you did not need.

title: Fixed coupon or percentage
hook: €5 off and 20% off cross over at a particular basket size.
question: A fictional basket can receive either 20% off or €5 off, with no exclusions. At €20, which final total is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional offers; one coupon only.
details: A fictional basket can receive either 20% off or €5 off, with no exclusions.
principle: The percentage scales with the basket; the fixed deduction does not. Their deductions match at €25 because 20% of €25 is €5. The lower result depends on the basket size.
objective: Find the crossover of fixed and percentage discounts.
misconception: A percentage discount is always larger than a fixed coupon.

recall.question: A fictional basket can take either 20% off or €5 off. From what basket total does 20% off give the lower final total?
options: €5 off is lower at every basket
20% off is lower at every basket
recall.why: 20% of €25 is €5; below that the fixed €5 removes more, above it the percentage does, so the answer depends on basket size.

title: The free-shipping gap
hook: Adding an item can remove shipping while raising the total you pay.
question: Shipping costs €4 below €50. B adds exactly enough merchandise to reach €50. At a €42 basket, which checkout is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional policy; added goods optional.
details: Shipping costs €4 below €50. B adds exactly enough merchandise to reach €50.
principle: Removing a shipping line is not the same as reducing the whole receipt. At €42, shipping makes €46; reaching €50 adds €8 of goods. Compare totals before naming a saving.
objective: Compare total checkout cost when adding merchandise to reach a shipping threshold.
misconception: Free shipping means a lower checkout total.

recall.question: Fictional shipping costs €4 below €50. Your basket is €44. Compared with paying shipping, adding goods to reach €50 makes the checkout total:
recall.why: Paying shipping totals €48; reaching €50 totals €50. Removing the shipping line is not the same as lowering the receipt.

title: One fixed fee per order
hook: The same goods can produce different totals when a fee repeats.
question: The same goods total €24. Each order adds a fictional €4 delivery fee. For two separate orders, which receipt is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; same goods; €4/order; no discounts.
details: The same goods total €24. Each order adds a fictional €4 delivery fee.
principle: A fixed fee repeats with each order. Combining changes the number of fees in this toy policy, not the merchandise subtotal. Count how many times each line is charged.
objective: Separate per-order charges from per-item costs.
misconception: Equal merchandise subtotals guarantee equal checkout totals.

recall.question: The same goods total €24, and each order adds a fictional €4 delivery fee. Placing three orders instead of one adds how much to the receipts?
recall.why: The fee repeats per order: three orders pay three fees, one order pays one, a difference of two fees (€8).

title: The voucher has a minimum
hook: A €5 voucher can leave a small basket unchanged.
question: A fictional voucher subtracts €5 only when the basket is at least €30. At €28, how do the totals compare?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional rule; €30 qualifying minimum.
details: A fictional voucher subtracts €5 only when the basket is at least €30.
principle: The threshold is part of the rule. Below €30 the deduction is zero; at €30 it becomes €5. An advertised deduction cannot be applied before checking eligibility.
objective: Apply a discontinuous minimum-purchase rule accurately.
misconception: Every basket gets the advertised voucher deduction.

recall.question: A fictional voucher takes €5 off only when the basket is at least €30. What does a €29 basket cost?
recall.why: €29 is below the threshold, so the deduction is zero; eligibility comes before the advertised discount.

title: Two discounts do not add
hook: 20% off, then 10% off: is that a 30% price cut?
question: A applies 20% off and then 10% off the reduced price. B applies 30% off once. At an original €100, which final price is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional offers; no other fees.
details: A applies 20% off and then 10% off the reduced price. B applies 30% off once.
principle: The second percentage acts on what remains. Multiplying 0.8 by 0.9 leaves 0.72 of the original price, not 0.70. The changed base explains the gap on the receipts.
objective: Calculate sequential discounts from the reduced base.
misconception: Sequential percentage reductions add directly.

recall.question: A fictional €200 item gets 20% off, then 10% off the reduced price. What is the final price?
recall.why: The second discount acts on €160, leaving 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72 of €200, not 0.70.

title: The discount round trip
hook: 20% down, then 20% up: will the price return to its starting point?
question: B reduces the original price by 20%, then raises that reduced price by 20%. At an original €100, where does B finish?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional prices; changing percentage base.
details: B reduces the original price by 20%, then raises that reduced price by 20%.
principle: The rise starts from the smaller base. Multiplying 0.8 by 1.2 gives 0.96, so the round trip finishes below the starting price. Equal percentages need not be equal amounts.
objective: Explain why opposite percentage changes do not cancel.
misconception: Equal percentage increases and decreases cancel out.

recall.question: A fictional €50 price falls by 20%, then rises by 20%. Where does it finish?
recall.why: The rise starts from €40, so it adds €8, not €10: 0.8 × 1.2 = 0.96 of the start.

title: Price per item you actually use
hook: A ten-pack can have a lower sticker price per piece and a higher cost per used piece.
question: Singles cost €0.50 each. A ten-pack costs €4. Unused pieces receive zero value in this model. If five pieces are used, which cost per used piece is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; unused pieces valued zero; fictional prices.
details: Singles cost €0.50 each. A ten-pack costs €4. Unused pieces receive zero value in this model.
principle: Here the relevant denominator is pieces used, not pieces purchased. Paying €4 and using five gives €0.80 per used piece. The model changes if the remaining pieces have value later.
objective: Distinguish purchase unit price from cost per utilized unit.
misconception: Lower cost per purchased piece guarantees lower cost per used piece.

recall.question: Singles cost €0.50 each; a ten-pack costs €4 and unused pieces count for nothing. How many pieces must you use before the ten-pack's cost per used piece falls to €0.50?
recall.why: Divide by pieces used, not bought: €4 ÷ 8 = €0.50; with fewer used, each used piece costs more.

title: Checkout cost versus net cost
hook: A refundable deposit changes checkout cash without changing the modeled net price.
question: Each item is €2.40 plus a fictional €0.25 deposit, refunded in full on return. For four items, which amount is higher?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional deposit; full return assumed.
details: Each item is €2.40 plus a fictional €0.25 deposit, refunded in full on return.
principle: The checkout includes a deposit for each container. The after-return amount subtracts those same deposits. These are different moments in the arithmetic; the scenario does not describe any region’s actual deposit law.
objective: Separate upfront deposits from net cost after a stated full refund.
misconception: Upfront cash paid and net cost after refunds are always the same.

recall.question: Each item is €2.40 plus a fictional €0.25 deposit, refunded in full on return. You buy ten and return all ten containers. What are the checkout and after-return amounts?
recall.why: The checkout includes ten €0.25 deposits; the return takes the same €2.50 back. They are two different moments.

title: Scale the portions, not the pan
hook: A four-portion recipe uses 300g. How much corresponds to six portions?
question: The quantity-only recipe uses 300g for four equal portions. How many grams preserve the same amount per portion for six portions?
assumptions: Scaled model; quantities only.
details: The quantity-only recipe uses 300g for four equal portions.
principle: The original rate is 75g per portion. Multiply that rate by the new portion count to keep the same amount per person. This demonstrates proportional quantity arithmetic, not cooking or nutritional advice.
objective: Scale a recipe quantity while preserving quantity per portion.
misconception: The same ingredient quantity serves more people without changing portion size.

recall.question: A quantity-only recipe uses 300g for four equal portions. How many grams keep the same amount per portion for two portions?
recall.why: The rate is 75g per portion; two portions × 75g = 150g. This is proportional quantity arithmetic only.

warning: Cooking times do not scale in proportion to quantity: follow the recipe's own times and check food is cooked through.

title: Round the pack, keep the remainder
hook: Three items per guest, ten per pack: how much extra appears?
question: Each guest receives three items. Packs contain ten items and cannot be split at purchase. For seven guests, which count is larger?
assumptions: Scaled model; quantity-only model; indivisible ten-packs.
details: Each guest receives three items. Packs contain ten items and cannot be split at purchase.
principle: First compute the exact requirement, then divide by pack size and round up. Purchased quantity is a multiple of ten. The gap is an explicit remainder rather than a change in portions.
objective: Round purchases to whole packs and compute excess quantity.
misconception: Buying whole packs provides exactly the required quantity.

recall.question: Each guest gets three items; packs hold ten and cannot be split. For nine guests, how many items are bought?
recall.why: Nine guests need 27; divide by ten and round up to three packs, so 30 are bought and 3 are left over.

title: Equal people, unequal portions
hook: Two full portions and one half portion: what does one full portion represent?
question: Two full portions and one half portion total 2.5 portion units. A splits by units; B by three people. At €30, which assigns more to a full-portion share?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional bill; agreed portion weights.
details: Two full portions and one half portion total 2.5 portion units. A splits by units; B by three people.
principle: A weighted split divides by 2.5 portion units rather than three people. A full portion gets one unit; the half portion gets half a unit. This is arithmetic under an agreed rule, not a recommendation for splitting bills.
objective: Calculate a weighted share and distinguish it from equal-person division.
misconception: Equal headcounts and equal consumption weights always produce the same split.

recall.question: A fictional €50 bill is split by portion units: two full portions and one half portion. What does each full portion pay?
recall.why: There are 2.5 portion units, so one unit is €50 ÷ 2.5 = €20; dividing by three people uses a different rule.

title: The leftover after equal shares
hook: Ten objects among three people: where does the tenth go?
question: Three recipients each receive the same whole-number count. Remainders are kept aside. At ten objects, which count is larger?
assumptions: Scaled model; whole objects; three equal shares.
details: Three recipients each receive the same whole-number count. Remainders are kept aside.
principle: Floor division makes equal whole-number shares, but it can leave a remainder. Ten gives three each and one aside. A remainder has to stay in the inventory even when it cannot fit the equal-share rule.
objective: Preserve the remainder after dividing indivisible resources equally.
misconception: Equal whole-number shares distribute every object automatically.

recall.question: Three recipients each get the same whole-number count; remainders stay aside. With 14 objects, how many stay aside?
recall.why: Floor division gives four each (12 objects); the 2 left over stay in the inventory.

title: Allocate by the stated weight
hook: Three trays have weights 2:1:1. Does an equal split follow those weights?
question: Three empty trays have allocation weights 2:1:1. Compare volume assigned to the first tray. At 8L total, which assigns more to tray one?
assumptions: Scaled model; empty trays; arithmetic allocation only.
details: Three empty trays have allocation weights 2:1:1. Compare volume assigned to the first tray.
principle: The weights add to four. The first tray receives two of four units, or half the total. Splitting into three equal shares uses a different rule and produces a different allocation.
objective: Allocate a conserved volume according to stated relative weights.
misconception: An equal split satisfies every weighted allocation rule.

recall.question: Three empty trays have allocation weights 2:1:1, and 12L is allocated. How much goes to tray one?
recall.why: The weights add to four and tray one holds two of them: half of 12L is 6L. An equal split would give 4L.

title: Coverage and whole containers
hook: A label says 8m² per litre. Fractional need is not a whole-container order.
question: A fictional coverage label states 8m² per litre. Containers hold 1L; coverage is assumed exact. For 10m², which volume is larger?
assumptions: Scaled model; hypothetical coverage; no application guidance.
details: A fictional coverage label states 8m² per litre. Containers hold 1L; coverage is assumed exact.
principle: Area divided by coverage gives modeled exact volume. The whole-container order rounds that result up. This ignores surface losses and product variation, so it teaches order arithmetic rather than actual application instructions.
objective: Distinguish continuous material need from indivisible container purchases.
misconception: A fractional material requirement can always be purchased exactly.

recall.question: A fictional label states 8m² per litre; containers hold 1L and cannot be split. How many containers for 17m²?
recall.why: 17 ÷ 8 = 2.125L exactly, and whole containers round that up to 3.

title: Ten extra or ten percent extra
hook: A fixed spare count and a percentage spare count diverge as a job grows.
question: Compare an order with 10% extra, rounded up, against an order with ten extra tiles. For 40 required tiles, which order is larger?
assumptions: Scaled model; quantity-only model; no installation advice.
details: Compare an order with 10% extra, rounded up, against an order with ten extra tiles.
principle: A fixed extra count stays ten. A percentage extra grows with the requirement. At forty, 10% is four; at one hundred, 10% is ten. Rounding up also ties them at 95; above 100 the percentage order is larger.
objective: Distinguish a proportional allowance from a fixed spare count.
misconception: Ten percent extra always means ten extra pieces.

recall.question: From what required count is 10% extra (rounded up) at least as large as ten extra?
recall.why: 10% grows with the requirement; the two orders are equal for requirements from 91 to 100 (95 and 100 on the slider), and below that ten extra is larger.

title: The allowance repeats each time
hook: Six panels each need a 5cm allowance. Is one 5cm allowance enough?
question: Each panel requires 1.20m plus a separate 0.05m allowance. Compare repeating the allowance with adding it once. For six panels, which modeled length is larger?
assumptions: Scaled model; length-only model; no cutting instructions.
details: Each panel requires 1.20m plus a separate 0.05m allowance. Compare repeating the allowance with adding it once.
principle: An allowance attached to every panel is a per-unit term. Multiply both the main length and allowance by the panel count. Adding the allowance once treats it as a single job-level term.
objective: Differentiate per-piece allowances from one-time allowances.
misconception: A per-piece allowance only needs to be added once.

recall.question: Each panel needs 1.20m plus its own 0.05m allowance. What total length do ten panels need?
recall.why: The allowance is per panel, so it is multiplied by ten too: 10 × 1.25m = 12.50m.

title: Stock during a delivery delay
hook: Four units leave daily. A longer lead time changes the reorder arithmetic.
question: Four units leave each day. After ordering, delivery takes three days. A must still have eight units when it arrives; B keeps no reserve. How many units must be on hand when ordering for A?
assumptions: Scaled model; constant toy demand; buffer=8; no policy advice.
details: Four units leave each day. After ordering, delivery takes three days. A must still have eight units when it arrives; B keeps no reserve.
principle: Multiply daily use by waiting days, then add the reserve. This is the stock left when ordering under the toy rule, not the quantity to buy. Real demand and delays can vary; the rule is illustrative.
objective: Calculate the stock on hand when ordering to cover a stated delivery delay and retain a stated reserve.
misconception: Delivery lead time has no effect on the quantity consumed before arrival.

recall.question: Five units leave each day and delivery takes four days after ordering. To still have six units when it arrives, how many must be on hand when you order?
recall.why: Use during the wait (5 × 4 = 20) plus the reserve of 6 gives 26.

title: Subtract what is already there
hook: Seven in stock and twelve needed: how many are missing?
question: Seven usable units are already available. A orders only the gap; B orders the whole requirement. At twelve required units, which order is smaller?
assumptions: Scaled model; usable stock=7; no hidden commitments.
details: Seven usable units are already available. A orders only the gap; B orders the whole requirement.
principle: Required quantity minus available stock gives the shortage. The maximum with zero prevents a negative order when stock already covers demand. Existing usable units belong in the calculation.
objective: Calculate nonnegative replenishment after counting available stock.
misconception: A shopping requirement is always the quantity that must be ordered.

recall.question: You need nine units and already have twelve usable ones. How many do you order?
recall.why: The order is the shortage, need minus stock, and never below zero: stock already covers the need.

title: On the shelf is not all free
hook: Six units are promised. Can every unit on the shelf serve a new request?
question: Six on-shelf units are already committed to earlier requests. Compare free and physical counts. At ten on-shelf units, which count is smaller?
assumptions: Scaled model; six committed; no incoming stock.
details: Six on-shelf units are already committed to earlier requests. Compare free and physical counts.
principle: Subtract committed units from the physical count to find free units. Commitments do not make the objects disappear, but they change which requests those objects can satisfy.
objective: Separate physical inventory from uncommitted availability.
misconception: Every item physically present is available for a new request.

recall.question: Fifteen units are on the shelf and nine are already promised to earlier requests. How many can a new request take?
recall.why: Free units are physical minus committed: 15 − 9 = 6. The promised units are present but not available.

title: Subtract stock before rounding
hook: Boxes hold six. Does twelve required mean ordering two boxes?
question: Three usable units are in stock. New orders come only in six-unit boxes. At twelve required, which new quantity is larger?
assumptions: Scaled model; stock=3; indivisible six-unit boxes.
details: Three usable units are in stock. New orders come only in six-unit boxes.
principle: Compute the shortage first, then round that shortage to whole boxes. Rounding the total requirement before subtracting stock uses the wrong input. Extra units after delivery remain visible in the count.
objective: Apply package rounding to the shortage rather than total demand.
misconception: Package rounding should be applied before existing stock is subtracted.

recall.question: Five usable units are in stock; new stock comes only in boxes of six. You need fourteen. How many units do you order?
recall.why: Compute the shortage first (14 − 5 = 9), then round that up to whole boxes: two boxes, 12 units.

title: A spare elsewhere changes the gap
hook: Two here, five freely available there: how many new units are missing?
question: There are two usable local units and five uncommitted units elsewhere that can be transferred at zero modeled cost. For ten required units, which external order is smaller?
assumptions: Scaled model; transfer allowed; zero modeled transfer cost.
details: There are two usable local units and five uncommitted units elsewhere that can be transferred at zero modeled cost.
principle: Pooling available stock changes the shortage from requirement minus two to requirement minus seven. The result depends on those other units actually being free and transferable under the stated assumptions.
objective: Account for transferable surplus before computing external replenishment.
misconception: Only items already in the destination count toward its shortage.

recall.question: Three usable units are here and four free units elsewhere can be transferred at no modeled cost. You need ten. How many must be ordered from outside?
recall.why: Pooled stock is 3 + 4 = 7, so the shortage is 10 − 7 = 3, provided those four are truly free to transfer.

title: Merge lists without counting twice
hook: Two requests overlap on three items. Adding the list lengths overcounts.
question: List A has eight distinct items; list B has six. Exactly three items occur on both lists. At A=8 items, which merged count is smaller?
assumptions: Scaled model; exact three-item overlap; unique items per list.
details: List A has eight distinct items; list B has six. Exactly three items occur on both lists.
principle: Count the overlap once, not twice. Adding list sizes includes the shared items in both lists, so subtract their shared count once. This assumes each individual list already has no duplicates.
objective: Use inclusion-exclusion for two overlapping resource lists.
misconception: The size of a merged list is always the sum of both list lengths.

recall.question: List A has ten distinct items and list B has seven; four items are on both. How many unique items does the merged list have?
recall.why: Adding gives 17 but counts the four shared items twice; subtract them once: 13.

title: Use the tickets with a deadline
hook: Six tickets expire after this event. Which choice leaves fewer of them unused?
question: Six tickets expire at the event’s end. Six others remain valid later. Use four before the deadline. Which choice leaves fewer expiring tickets unused?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional tickets; equal acceptance; no food guidance.
details: Six tickets expire at the event’s end. Six others remain valid later. Use four before the deadline.
principle: Using deadline tickets first reduces the expiring remainder. Using the other tickets leaves all six deadline tickets unused. This is a declared ticket-validity model, not guidance about food or unsafe expired goods.
objective: Choose among equivalent resources using a stated expiration deadline.
misconception: Equivalent resources have identical consequences regardless of deadline.

recall.question: Five tickets expire tonight; five others stay valid later. You use three tonight, choosing the expiring ones first. How many expiring tickets go unused?
recall.why: Using the expiring tickets first leaves 5 − 3 = 2 to expire; using the others first would leave all 5.

title: A count correction travels forward
hook: The record says ten, the shelf has eight. Which count remains after shipping three?
question: The physical count is two below the record. Three units are then dispatched. At a record of ten, which remaining count is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; count difference=2; dispatch=3; no receipts.
details: The physical count is two below the record. Three units are then dispatched.
principle: Subtract the discrepancy before updating the dispatch. Shipping three from an already incorrect record preserves its two-unit error. A corrected observation needs to travel into the next calculation.
objective: Propagate a counted inventory discrepancy through a later transaction.
misconception: A later dispatch automatically fixes an earlier inventory error.

recall.question: The record says 20 units, but a physical count finds 17. You then dispatch four. How many are really left?
recall.why: Correct the record to the count first (17), then subtract the dispatch: 13. The record's 16 keeps the old error.

title: Power and duration trade places
hook: 100W for one hour or 20W for five: compare the energy, not just watts.
question: Illustrative A runs at 100W for one hour; B at 20W for five hours. B’s duration stays five times A’s. At A=1h, which uses more energy?
assumptions: Scaled model; illustrative:100W×h;20W×5h;tariff=€0.30/kWh.
details: Illustrative A runs at 100W for one hour; B at 20W for five hours. B’s duration stays five times A’s.
principle: Energy is power multiplied by duration. Here the fivefold duration exactly offsets the fivefold power difference. A low watt number alone cannot identify the lower energy total.
objective: Compare energy use while accounting for both constant power and duration.
misconception: Lower power always means lower total energy consumption.

recall.question: Illustrative loads: 50W for two hours, or 10W for ten hours. Which uses more energy?
recall.why: Energy is power × time: both are 100Wh (0.1kWh), so the lower watt number alone did not decide it.

warning: Tariffs and appliance ratings vary: check your own.

title: Long idle, short active
hook: A small load lasts many hours. Does duration make it larger than the active load?
question: Illustrative daily loads: active 60W for 2h, idle 3W for 22h. Constant power is assumed. Over five days, which modeled energy total is higher?
assumptions: Scaled model; illustrative:60W×2h/day;3W×22h/day;€0.30/kWh.
details: Illustrative daily loads: active 60W for 2h, idle 3W for 22h. Constant power is assumed.
principle: Multiply each power by its own duration before comparing. The longer idle period contributes energy, yet under these stated numbers it remains below active use. No actual appliance rating is implied.
objective: Compare separate operating-state energy contributions.
misconception: The state lasting the most hours must consume the most energy.

recall.question: Illustrative day: active 40W for 1 hour, idle 2W for 23 hours. Which state uses more energy that day?
recall.why: Multiply each power by its own hours: active 40Wh, idle 46Wh. Neither the bigger wattage nor the longer time decides it alone.

warning: Tariffs and appliance ratings vary: check your own.

title: A tiny load accumulates
hook: Two watts over a whole day and over one hour are different annual totals.
question: A constant illustrative 2W load runs for either 24h/day or 1h/day. Over 365 days, which accumulates more energy?
assumptions: Scaled model; illustrative:2W;24h/day-or-1h/day;€0.30/kWh.
details: A constant illustrative 2W load runs for either 24h/day or 1h/day.
principle: A daily amount repeats across days. The formula multiplies watts, hours per day, and days before dividing by one thousand. It describes a hypothetical constant load and does not instruct you to disconnect safety-critical equipment.
objective: Convert a small stated constant load into a multiday energy quantity.
misconception: A small wattage cannot accumulate a meaningful quantity over many days.

recall.question: An illustrative constant 3W load runs 24 hours a day for 365 days. About how much energy does it accumulate?
recall.why: 3W × 24h × 365 days = 26,280Wh, about 26.3kWh: a small daily amount repeats every day.

warning: Tariffs and appliance ratings vary: check your own.

title: Rated power and active time
hook: A hypothetical load runs only one quarter of each hour. Should every hour use full power?
question: Illustrative power is 100W when on and 0W when off. A runs one quarter of the time; B continuously. Over eight hours, which modeled energy total is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; illustrative:100W-on;0W-off;25%-or-100%;€0.30/kWh.
details: Illustrative power is 100W when on and 0W when off. A runs one quarter of the time; B continuously.
principle: Multiply elapsed time by the on-time fraction before applying constant on-power. A nameplate-sized number cannot replace the duration actually spent at that power in this toy model.
objective: Use a stated duty fraction rather than treating rated power as continuous.
misconception: Every elapsed hour must be charged at full on-state power.

recall.question: An illustrative load draws 200W when on and 0W when off. It is on half the time over ten hours. How much energy does it use?
recall.why: Charge only the on-time: 200W × (0.5 × 10h) = 1,000Wh = 1kWh, not 2kWh for the whole ten hours.

title: The fixed charge changes the bill
hook: A lower per-kWh price can still produce a higher total at small usage.
question: Fictional tariff A is €0.20/kWh plus €10. B is €0.30/kWh without a fixed charge. At 40kWh, which modeled bill is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional:€0.20/kWh+€10;€0.30/kWh;no taxes.
details: Fictional tariff A is €0.20/kWh plus €10. B is €0.30/kWh without a fixed charge.
principle: A lower variable rate does not erase a fixed charge. At 40kWh, A totals €18 and B €12. They match at 100kWh under these exact assumptions; real tariffs can include other terms.
objective: Compare fixed and usage-dependent charges in a stated bill model.
misconception: The smallest per-kWh rate always makes the smallest total bill.

recall.question: Fictional tariff A is €0.20/kWh plus €10; tariff B is €0.30/kWh with no fixed charge. Above what usage is A's bill lower?
options: A is lower at every usage
recall.why: A's €10 fixed charge is recovered at €0.10 per kWh saved, so the bills match at 100kWh; below that, B is lower.

warning: Tariffs and appliance ratings vary: check your own.

title: Same energy, different tariff
hook: Moving a hypothetical load changes its price while leaving its energy unchanged.
question: The same 3kWh is billed at fictional rates of €0.40/kWh or €0.20/kWh, with no other charges. Which modeled cost is lower at 3kWh?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional:€0.40/kWh-or-€0.20/kWh;same kWh.
details: The same 3kWh is billed at fictional rates of €0.40/kWh or €0.20/kWh, with no other charges.
principle: The cost changes because the price multiplier changes. The energy quantity stays the same. This isolates tariff arithmetic and does not imply that every load can safely or practically move to another time.
objective: Distinguish a cost change from an energy-use change.
misconception: A lower electricity charge necessarily means fewer kilowatt-hours were used.

recall.question: A modeled bill falls from €2.40 to €1.20 because the same use moved from a fictional €0.40/kWh rate to €0.20/kWh. How much energy was used each time?
recall.why: €2.40 ÷ €0.40 = 6kWh and €1.20 ÷ €0.20 = 6kWh: the price changed, the energy did not.

warning: Tariffs and appliance ratings vary: check your own.

title: Read the annual-energy number
hook: Two illustrative annual labels differ. How does that difference repeat over years?
question: Illustrative annual quantities are 200kWh and 350kWh. Both are priced at €0.30/kWh every year. At two years, which modeled running cost is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; illustrative:200-or-350kWh/year;€0.30/kWh;constant years.
details: Illustrative annual quantities are 200kWh and 350kWh. Both are priced at €0.30/kWh every year.
principle: Multiply annual energy by years and the stated unit price. This extrapolation assumes unchanged use and tariff; it is not a measured forecast for a named product.
objective: Translate a stated annual energy figure into a multiyear running-cost model.
misconception: An annual energy label is already the multiyear cost.

recall.question: An illustrative label states 250kWh per year. At an unchanged fictional €0.30/kWh, what is the modeled running cost over four years?
recall.why: Annual energy × years × price: 250 × 4 × €0.30 = €300. The label is one year, not the multiyear cost.

title: Price tag plus running cost
hook: A higher upfront price can cross a lower one after repeated running costs.
question: Illustrative A costs €80 plus 120kWh/year. B costs €140 plus 60kWh/year. Electricity is €0.30/kWh. At two years, which modeled total is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; illustrative:€80+120kWh/y;€140+60kWh/y;€0.30/kWh.
details: Illustrative A costs €80 plus 120kWh/year. B costs €140 plus 60kWh/year. Electricity is €0.30/kWh.
principle: Add the upfront term to repeated running costs. A starts lower, while B’s modeled running cost grows more slowly. This arithmetic omits repair, lifespan and discounting and is not a purchasing recommendation.
objective: Combine an upfront amount and repeated operating charges without assuming the same winner at every horizon.
misconception: The lower initial price guarantees a lower total at every future horizon.

recall.question: Illustrative A costs €80 plus 120kWh/year; B costs €140 plus 60kWh/year; electricity is a fictional €0.30/kWh. When does B's total become lower?
recall.why: B starts €60 higher but saves 60kWh × €0.30 = €18 a year, so it catches up after €60 ÷ €18 ≈ 3.3 years.

title: Flow times minutes
hook: A flow rate is not the final volume until duration joins it.
question: Two hypothetical constant flows are 6L/min and 3L/min, each running four minutes. Which modeled volume is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; illustrative constant flows; no fixture instructions.
details: Two hypothetical constant flows are 6L/min and 3L/min, each running four minutes.
principle: A volume per minute multiplied by minutes gives volume. Keeping duration equal isolates the flow-rate difference. Actual flow can vary, so the picture demonstrates the stated arithmetic only.
objective: Convert a constant flow rate and duration into volume.
misconception: Litres per minute already states total litres used.

recall.question: A hypothetical constant flow of 8L/min runs for five minutes. What volume does it deliver?
recall.why: Litres per minute × minutes = litres: 8 × 5 = 40L. The rate alone is not the total.

title: A slower flow runs longer
hook: Halving a flow rate and doubling duration: what happens to volume?
question: Hypothetical A is 12L/min for two minutes. B is 6L/min for twice A’s duration. At A=2min, which modeled volume is larger?
assumptions: Scaled model; illustrative:12L/min×t;6L/min×2t;constant flow.
details: Hypothetical A is 12L/min for two minutes. B is 6L/min for twice A’s duration.
principle: The half-rate and double-duration factors cancel. Both deliver the same modeled volume. A rate reduction by itself does not state the final volume when the duration also changes.
objective: Explain the offset between rate and duration under a fixed proportional change.
misconception: Half the flow rate always means half the volume.

recall.question: Hypothetical A runs at 10L/min for three minutes; B at 5L/min for six minutes. How do their volumes compare?
recall.why: Half the rate for twice the time cancels: both deliver 30L.

title: Fill time is not water saved
hook: A slower flow takes longer to fill the same bucket.
question: A fixed 10L volume is filled by hypothetical constant flows of 5L/min or 2.5L/min. No spills occur. Which modeled fill time is longer?
assumptions: Scaled model; illustrative rates; fixed volume; no spills.
details: A fixed 10L volume is filled by hypothetical constant flows of 5L/min or 2.5L/min. No spills occur.
principle: Divide the required volume by flow rate to get fill time. Both cases deliver the same bucket volume; the slower case only takes longer under these assumptions.
objective: Distinguish fixed-volume filling from fixed-duration water use.
misconception: A slower flow necessarily uses less water to fill a fixed container.

recall.question: A 12L container is filled by a hypothetical constant 4L/min or 2L/min flow, with no spills. How much water does the slower flow use?
recall.why: Both fill the same 12L; the slower flow only takes longer (6 minutes instead of 3).

title: Small flow, long duration
hook: A millilitre-per-minute amount repeats many more times in a day than in an hour.
question: A hypothetical constant 5mL/min flow continues for either one hour or one day. Which modeled volume is larger?
assumptions: Scaled model; illustrative constant flow; 24h/day; 1000mL/L.
details: A hypothetical constant 5mL/min flow continues for either one hour or one day.
principle: A day contains 1,440 minutes; an hour contains sixty. Multiply by the relevant minute count and convert millilitres to litres. A small rate and a long duration belong in the same calculation.
objective: Convert a small continuous flow to hourly and daily volumes.
misconception: A small rate remains a small total regardless of duration.

recall.question: A hypothetical constant 10mL/min flow runs for one whole day. What volume is that?
recall.why: A day is 1,440 minutes: 10mL × 1,440 = 14,400mL = 14.4L. A small rate and a long time belong in one calculation.

title: The whole-litre rounding gap
hook: 250mL per cup can leave a whole-litre fill above the exact requirement.
question: Each empty cup is allocated 250mL. Compare exact total volume with that total rounded up to whole litres. For five cups, which modeled volume is larger?
assumptions: Scaled model; empty cups; volume only; no heating guidance.
details: Each empty cup is allocated 250mL. Compare exact total volume with that total rounded up to whole litres.
principle: Multiply cup count by millilitres per cup, then convert to litres. Rounding up introduces an excess that is visible as the difference between the two results. Exact need and a coarse fill increment are different quantities.
objective: Compute excess created by rounding a volume to coarse increments.
misconception: A rounded fill volume always equals the exact serving volume.

recall.question: Each cup is allocated 250mL and the fill is rounded up to whole litres. For nine cups, how much is the excess over the exact need?
recall.why: Exact need is 9 × 250mL = 2.25L; rounding up gives 3L, an excess of 0.75L.

title: Litres and cubic metres
hook: A thousand litres is not a thousand cubic metres.
question: A converts litres to cubic metres by dividing by 1,000. B incorrectly keeps the same numeric digits. For 1,500L, which result has the correct cubic-metre unit?
assumptions: Scaled model; unit model; 1000L=1m³; B deliberately wrong.
details: A converts litres to cubic metres by dividing by 1,000. B incorrectly keeps the same numeric digits.
principle: Changing units can require changing the number. One cubic metre contains one thousand litres, so dividing by one thousand preserves the volume. Keeping the digits while changing the unit describes a different volume.
objective: Convert a meter quantity from litres to cubic metres.
misconception: A number can keep the same digits when its volume unit changes.

recall.question: A meter reading of 1,800 litres is converted to cubic metres. What is the correct value?
recall.why: One cubic metre holds 1,000 litres, so divide by 1,000: 1.8m³. Keeping the digits would describe a thousand times the volume.

title: Turn it; volume stays the same
hook: Swapping the height and width of an ideal box changes its drawing, not its capacity.
question: An ideal internal box measures 20cm by 10cm by 15cm. B exchanges the last two dimensions. Which modeled internal capacity is larger?
assumptions: Scaled model; ideal inner dimensions; 1000cm³/L.
details: An ideal internal box measures 20cm by 10cm by 15cm. B exchanges the last two dimensions.
principle: The same three lengths remain in the product. Multiplication does not depend on their order, so rotation preserves the ideal internal volume. Real fitting constraints can still depend on orientation.
objective: Separate ideal container capacity from the orientation of its dimensions.
misconception: Turning a rectangular box changes its ideal internal volume.

recall.question: An ideal box measures 30cm × 20cm × 10cm inside (6L). What happens to its internal capacity when it is turned onto another face?
options: It grows when stood on its smallest face
It shrinks when laid on its largest face
recall.why: Capacity is the product of the same three lengths, and order does not change a product; only fit can change.

title: Double the radius, not the volume
hook: Two ideal cylinders have equal height and radii of 3cm and 6cm.
question: Ideal cylinders have inner radii 3cm and 6cm; both have inner height 10cm. Which capacity is four times the other?
assumptions: Scaled model; ideal cylinders; V=πr²h; 1000cm³/L.
details: Ideal cylinders have inner radii 3cm and 6cm; both have inner height 10cm.
principle: Cylinder capacity depends on radius squared. Doubling radius multiplies the circular base area by four; equal height then gives four times the volume. The dimensions here are ideal internal measurements.
objective: Predict cylinder capacity scaling when radius doubles at fixed height.
misconception: Doubling radius only doubles an ideal cylinder’s capacity.

recall.question: Two ideal cylinders have equal height; one has radius 4cm and the other 12cm. How many times as much does the wider one hold?
recall.why: Capacity scales with radius squared: three times the radius gives 3² = 9 times the base area and volume.

title: Double the side, quadruple area
hook: Two square surfaces have side lengths 2m and 4m. Is the second only twice as large?
question: Compare an ideal square of side 2m with one of side 4m. B’s side remains twice A’s. Which area is four times the other?
assumptions: Scaled model; ideal squares; area=side×side.
details: Compare an ideal square of side 2m with one of side 4m. B’s side remains twice A’s.
principle: Both dimensions double, so the product gets a factor of two twice. Four times the area means four times the material in an ideal area-only coverage model, rather than twice.
objective: Apply square scaling to area coverage.
misconception: Doubling a square’s side only doubles the area to cover.

recall.question: An ideal square's side is halved, from 6m to 3m. What fraction of the original area is left to cover?
recall.why: Both dimensions halve, so area is multiplied by ½ twice: 36m² becomes 9m², one quarter.

title: Subtract the opening once
hook: A rectangular panel includes a 2m² opening. Counting the outline counts too much surface.
question: An ideal panel is 3m high and 4m wide, with one 2m² opening that needs no covering. Which area corresponds to the remaining surface?
assumptions: Scaled model; ideal dimensions; fixed 2m² opening.
details: An ideal panel is 3m high and 4m wide, with one 2m² opening that needs no covering.
principle: Multiply width by height for the outline, then subtract the opening’s area once. The outline is a boundary enclosing both material and empty space; it is not automatically the area needing coverage.
objective: Subtract a stated opening from rectangular coverage area.
misconception: The outer rectangle always equals the area requiring material.

recall.question: An ideal wall is 2.5m high and 5m wide, with two openings of 1.5m² each that need no covering. What area needs covering?
recall.why: Outline 12.5m² minus both openings (3m²) is 9.5m²; the outline includes empty space.

title: The overlap needs material too
hook: A 2cm overlap repeats along a 20cm edge. Where does its area go?
question: An ideal paper rectangle is 20cm long. Its 30cm width needs a further 2cm overlap. Which modeled paper area includes the overlap?
assumptions: Scaled model; ideal paper; overlap=2cm; no cutting guidance.
details: An ideal paper rectangle is 20cm long. Its 30cm width needs a further 2cm overlap.
principle: The extra strip has width two and length twenty, so it adds forty square centimetres. The overlap is material that exists even when it is hidden beneath another layer.
objective: Include a seam or overlap strip in area requirements.
misconception: Hidden overlap does not contribute to material area.

recall.question: An ideal paper rectangle is 25cm long. Its 40cm width needs a further 3cm overlap. What paper area is needed?
recall.why: The hidden overlap is a 3cm × 25cm strip, adding 75cm² to the 1,000cm²: 43 × 25 = 1,075cm².

title: Around is not across
hook: A perimeter measurement and a corner-to-corner measurement follow different paths.
question: An ideal rectangle is 4m wide and 3m high. Compare one full perimeter with one diagonal. Which path needs more length?
assumptions: Scaled model; ideal rectangle; length only.
details: An ideal rectangle is 4m wide and 3m high. Compare one full perimeter with one diagonal.
principle: Perimeter adds all four edges. The diagonal follows one straight corner-to-corner path and uses the square-root relationship. Name the route before calculating the required length; the same rectangle supports different measurements.
objective: Select the correct length formula for boundary versus corner-to-corner routes.
misconception: Every measurement associated with a rectangle is its perimeter.

recall.question: An ideal rectangle is 8m wide and 6m high. How long is one corner-to-corner diagonal?
recall.why: The diagonal is √(8² + 6²) = 10m; 28m is the perimeter, a different route.

title: When reuse catches up
hook: €12 once or €0.20 each use: when do their modeled costs per use match?
question: A reusable item costs €12 once. Equivalent single-use items cost €0.20 each. Ongoing costs are excluded. At fifty uses, which modeled cost per use is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional prices; upkeep excluded; equivalent service.
details: A reusable item costs €12 once. Equivalent single-use items cost €0.20 each. Ongoing costs are excluded.
principle: Divide a one-time amount by uses to obtain its modeled cost per use. Here it matches €0.20 at sixty uses. This omits upkeep, lifespan and environmental impacts and makes no purchasing recommendation.
objective: Find a reuse cost-per-use crossover under explicitly limited costs.
misconception: A reusable purchase is automatically cheaper at every use count.

recall.question: A reusable item costs €15 once; equivalent single-use items cost €0.25 each; ongoing costs are excluded. At how many uses do their costs per use match?
recall.why: €15 ÷ uses = €0.25 when uses = 60; below that, the reusable item costs more per use in this model.

title: The last sheet can be half-used
hook: Two pages per sheet: what happens when the page count is odd?
question: All pages can be printed one per side, either single-sided or on both sides. Blank final sides are allowed. For seven pages, which sheet count is smaller?
assumptions: Scaled model; page-count model; two printable sides/sheet.
details: All pages can be printed one per side, either single-sided or on both sides. Blank final sides are allowed.
principle: Divide pages by two and round up for double-sided sheets. An odd final page still occupies a whole sheet. The ceiling makes that partly unused final sheet visible instead of pretending it is half a physical sheet.
objective: Compute whole-sheet needs for odd double-sided page counts.
misconception: Double-sided printing always uses exactly half a sheet per page.

recall.question: Printing double-sided, with a blank final side allowed: how many sheets do eleven pages need?
recall.why: 11 ÷ 2 = 5.5, rounded up to 6: the odd last page still takes a whole sheet.

title: Two offcuts are not one long piece
hook: A 90cm piece and a 50cm piece cannot supply two unjoined 60cm lengths.
question: Unjoined usable pieces must each be 60cm. The available offcuts are 90cm and 50cm, with zero modeled cut loss. Which result represents usable separate pieces at 60cm?
assumptions: Scaled model; no joining; cut loss=0; lengths only.
details: Unjoined usable pieces must each be 60cm. The available offcuts are 90cm and 50cm, with zero modeled cut loss.
principle: Each required piece has to fit within one offcut. Count fits separately before adding them. Summing lengths first invents continuity between the two offcuts; the pooled result is an intentionally infeasible comparison.
objective: Respect indivisible stock-piece boundaries when counting reusable offcuts.
misconception: Adding offcut lengths makes them equivalent to one continuous piece.

recall.question: You have two offcuts of 70cm each and need unjoined pieces of 100cm. How many 100cm pieces can you cut?
recall.why: Each piece must fit inside one offcut, and neither is 100cm long; the pooled 140cm is not one continuous piece.

title: Count material, state the boundary
hook: A heavier reusable container and light replacements accumulate material differently.
question: A toy reusable container starts at 200g and uses 2g of replacement material/use. Single-use replacements each use 20g. At ten uses, which modeled material total is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; toy masses; material only; no lifecycle claim.
details: A toy reusable container starts at 200g and uses 2g of replacement material/use. Single-use replacements each use 20g.
principle: Include the starting material and the repeated additions within the chosen boundary. This toy mass account excludes energy, cleaning, transport and disposal; lower mass here does not establish a lower environmental impact.
objective: Compare cumulative material amounts while stating what the account excludes.
misconception: A material-mass comparison alone proves the lower environmental impact.

recall.question: Toy mass account: a reusable container is 200g plus 2g per use; each single-use replacement is 20g. From how many uses is the reusable total lower?
recall.why: At 11 uses it is 222g versus 220g; at 12 it is 224g versus 240g. Include the starting mass, and mass alone is not environmental impact.

title: Entry fee versus per-visit fee
hook: A fixed access fee and a smaller visit charge cross a pay-per-visit total.
question: Fictional A charges €10 per visit. B charges €30 once plus €4 per visit; service is assumed equivalent. At three visits, which modeled total is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional prices; equivalent service; no recommendation.
details: Fictional A charges €10 per visit. B charges €30 once plus €4 per visit; service is assumed equivalent.
principle: Separate the one-time term from the per-visit term. The two totals match at five visits in this model. The comparison does not determine which service fits someone’s needs or predict future attendance.
objective: Calculate a fixed-access versus per-visit crossover.
misconception: A smaller per-visit charge guarantees a smaller total.

recall.question: Fictional A charges €9 per visit; B charges €24 once plus €5 per visit. At how many visits do the totals match?
recall.why: B's €24 one-time fee is recovered at €4 per visit, so totals match at 6 visits (€54 each).

title: Billing rounds the quantity
hook: Three and a half hours can be billed as four complete hours.
question: Fictional A charges €4 per begun hour. B charges €20 per begun 24h period. At 3.5h, which modeled bill is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional rules; each begun unit billed.
details: Fictional A charges €4 per begun hour. B charges €20 per begun 24h period.
principle: The billing unit can differ from measured duration. A rounds each begun hour upward; B rounds each begun day upward. Apply the declared rounding rule before multiplying by its price.
objective: Apply billing increments and ceiling rules to fractional duration.
misconception: A partial hour is always billed as the exact fraction used.

recall.question: Fictional A charges €4 per begun hour; B charges €20 per begun 24-hour period. At 5.5 hours, which bill is lower?
recall.why: 5.5 hours bills as 6 begun hours (€24) against one begun day (€20): apply each rounding rule before pricing.

title: A bundle includes unused tickets
hook: Five-ticket bundles can force a second bundle for the sixth trip.
question: Fictional singles cost €2. A five-ticket bundle costs €8 and cannot be split; leftover tickets are unused here. For six trips, which checkout is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional fares; leftover value=0; no recommendation.
details: Fictional singles cost €2. A five-ticket bundle costs €8 and cannot be split; leftover tickets are unused here.
principle: A sixth required trip needs a second complete bundle under this rule. The checkout pays for unused tickets too. Effective use count and purchased count are different denominators.
objective: Compare exact-demand tickets with indivisible ticket bundles.
misconception: A discounted bundle is cheaper for every required trip count.

recall.question: Fictional singles cost €2; a five-ticket bundle costs €8 and cannot be split. For eleven trips using bundles only, what is the checkout?
recall.why: Eleven trips need three whole bundles (€24), more than eleven singles (€22): unused tickets are paid for.

title: One parcel fee, many item charges
hook: A fixed parcel fee is different from a fee attached to each item.
question: A fictional parcel costs €3 plus €0.50 per item. Items can share one parcel or each use a parcel. For four items, which charge is lower?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional policy; shared parcel permitted; no other fees.
details: A fictional parcel costs €3 plus €0.50 per item. Items can share one parcel or each use a parcel.
principle: The per-item charge repeats either way, but the fixed parcel fee repeats only with separate parcels. Labeling a cost as fixed requires naming the thing it is fixed per.
objective: Separate per-parcel overhead from per-item charges when aggregating shipments.
misconception: Combining parcels removes every charge, including per-item charges.

recall.question: A fictional parcel costs €3 plus €0.50 per item. Shipping ten items in ten separate parcels instead of one costs how much more?
recall.why: The per-item charge is the same either way; only the €3 parcel fee repeats, nine extra times: €27.

title: Average the quantities too
hook: Mixing different quantities makes a simple average of unit prices misleading.
question: Material A costs €3/kg and B €6/kg. Compare 1kg of each with 2kg A plus 1kg B. Which mixture has the lower average price at A=2kg?
assumptions: Scaled model; fictional prices; additive masses; no mixing guidance.
details: Material A costs €3/kg and B €6/kg. Compare 1kg of each with 2kg A plus 1kg B.
principle: Total price divided by total mass weights each unit price by its quantity. The simple mean of €3 and €6 only describes equal masses. A larger share of the cheaper material shifts the weighted mean downward.
objective: Compute a quantity-weighted average rather than averaging unit prices blindly.
misconception: A mixture’s average unit price is always the simple mean of its labels.

recall.question: Fictional material A is €2/kg and B is €8/kg. You combine 3kg of A with 1kg of B. What is the average price per kilogram?
recall.why: Total price ÷ total mass: (€6 + €8) ÷ 4kg = €3.50. The simple mean (€5) only holds for equal masses.

title: Capacity changes batch count
hook: Twenty objects and a six-object carrier: a remainder still needs another trip.
question: Ideal carriers hold exactly six or eight identical objects. Objects cannot be split; capacity is assumed usable. For twenty objects, which needs fewer batches?
assumptions: Scaled model; ideal usable capacities; no weight or safety claim.
details: Ideal carriers hold exactly six or eight identical objects. Objects cannot be split; capacity is assumed usable.
principle: Divide object count by usable capacity and round up. The partial final batch still counts as a complete trip in this quantity-only model. Volume, weight and safe carrying limits would require separate constraints.
objective: Calculate whole batch counts using a stated usable capacity.
misconception: A fractional last batch can be ignored when counting trips.

recall.question: Ideal carriers hold exactly eight identical objects, which cannot be split. How many batches do 25 objects need?
recall.why: 25 ÷ 8 = 3.125, and the partial last batch is still a whole trip: 4.

title: Move the decimal with the unit
hook: 125 cents is not €12.50. The unit tells you the conversion factor.
question: A euro contains 100 cents. A divides cents by 100; B deliberately divides by ten instead. For 125 cents, which conversion is correct?
assumptions: Scaled model; unit arithmetic; 100 cents/€; B deliberately wrong.
details: A euro contains 100 cents. A divides cents by 100; B deliberately divides by ten instead.
principle: The denominator comes from the unit definition: one hundred cents per euro. Dividing by ten changes the amount by the wrong factor. Carry the unit alongside the digits so the decimal movement has a reason.
objective: Convert cents to euros using the stated unit relationship.
misconception: Converting cents to euros requires moving the decimal only one place.

recall.question: A euro is 100 cents. How many euros is 305 cents?
recall.why: Divide by 100, the number of cents per euro: €3.05. Dividing by ten gives €30.50.

title: Round lines or round the total
hook: Rounding three tiny lines separately can differ from rounding their sum once.
question: Each fictional line is exactly €0.335 before rounding. A rounds each line to cents; B sums first and rounds once. For three lines, which modeled result is higher?
assumptions: Scaled model; toy rule: nearest cent, half upward; no billing-law claim.
details: Each fictional line is exactly €0.335 before rounding. A rounds each line to cents; B sums first and rounds once.
principle: Rounding loses information at each application. Three rounded €0.34 lines sum to €1.02, while €1.005 rounded once gives €1.01 under the stated half-up rule. Actual billing conventions need their own rule.
objective: Compare line-level rounding with aggregate rounding under a stated convention.
misconception: Rounding before summing is always identical to rounding after summing.

recall.question: Four fictional lines are each exactly €0.125, rounded half-up to cents. What do you get rounding each line first, and rounding the total once?
recall.why: Each line rounds to €0.13, so four make €0.52; the exact total €0.50 needs no rounding. Rounding loses information each time.
